In his piece for Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Marcus Theurer describes Europe's near-total dependence on China for solar technology, alongside a new attempt to build a billion-euro "Gigafactory" in Hambach, Alsace, that would combine European political protection with technological partnership with Chinese firms. The article frames the project's fate as hinging on upcoming EU trade and industrial-policy decisions, and quotes industry voices arguing that protective European regulation is essential if domestic manufacturing is to grow. As no other source addresses this topic, there is no cross-source contrast to draw.

6907.topic_label: Sovereign wealth funds and financial geopolitics
6907.comparison_text: Only one source addresses this topic. In his article in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Franz Nestler examines Norway's sovereign wealth fund, built from oil and gas revenues, highlighting its unusual transparency and scale, and situates it in a broader comparison with other major sovereign funds from the Middle East, Asia, Turkey, Canada and the US state of Alaska. He frames such funds' investment decisions as a matter of geopolitical and financial influence that extends well beyond their home countries, but since no other outlet covers this topic, there is no competing emphasis or counter-framing to compare it against.

6908.topic_label: German medical technology industry vs Chinese competition
6908.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In his article for Die Welt, Andreas Macho frames the situation as a "China shock 2.0," arguing that German medical technology firms are under mounting competitive pressure from Chinese manufacturers who are flooding export markets with advanced, low-cost devices while China shields its own domestic market through discriminatory procurement rules that disadvantage foreign companies. The piece also raises a security dimension, warning of possible data-security risks posed by Chinese-made medical devices, and cites industry voices describing firms as deeply alarmed. Since no other source covers this topic, there is no cross-newspaper contrast to draw - the article itself combines an economic-competitiveness angle with a strategic-security angle.

6909.topic_label: Semiconductor shortage driven by AI data center boom
6909.comparison_text: This topic is covered by only one source. In his piece for Die Welt, Andreas Macho describes how the surging demand for chips and components to build AI data centers is pulling resources away from other industries, particularly automotive manufacturing, producing shortages, price spikes, and even production stoppages reminiscent of the COVID-era supply chain crisis. The article quotes suppliers warning that major customers are trying to buy up their entire production capacity for the next five years, and cautions that the situation could escalate further if the shortages spread to critical infrastructure.

6910.topic_label: German academia and bias on the Middle East conflict
6910.comparison_text: Both pieces appear in Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung as signed academic contributions and share a common concern about the disappearance of pluralism in German academia regarding the Middle East conflict, though each approaches it from a different angle. In his column, Professor Klaus Ries argues that scientific objectivity was always something of an illusion, but warns that the real danger now is that almost no diversity of opinion remains - academic discourse on the conflict, he writes, is dominated almost exclusively by pro-Palestinian and anti-Israel positions, which he characterizes as effectively antisemitic, and which he sees as undermining the very foundations of democracy. By contrast, in his letter, Professor Jens Peter Laut narrows the focus to a specific field - Turkology - describing how ideological bias now makes it difficult to acknowledge the contributions of major Israeli scholars such as Uriel Heyd and Jacob Landau, to the point that he fears he could scarcely mention them in his lectures except pejoratively. While Ries offers a broad, systemic diagnosis of the state of pluralism across German academia, Laut provides a more personal and narrowly focused illustration from his own discipline, yet both converge on the same underlying claim: that a wider trend of politicization is eroding academic freedom.

6911.topic_label: Culture war within the US military
6911.comparison_text: This topic is covered by only one source, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, in an unsigned piece reflecting the newspaper's own institutional stance. It examines Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's campaign against "woke culture," diversity and inclusion policies, and what he portrays as the corrosive influence of the "Frankfurt School" on American military readiness. The article frames Hegseth's rhetoric as deeply ironic: the very Frankfurt School émigrés he targets - Herbert Marcuse, Franz Neumann and Otto Kirchheimer - had actually worked for the US government through the OSS to help understand and defeat Nazism. The piece thus presents Hegseth's attack as unwittingly mirroring the authoritarian logic it claims to oppose. Since no other outlet addresses this story, there is no competing frame to compare, only this single critical reading of the episode.

6912.topic_label: Classical antiquity as political ideology among US tech elites
6912.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, in a column by Niklas Maak. Maak argues that figures such as Rubio, Vance, Thiel, Musk and Bezos are instrumentalizing a mythologized, purified vision of Greco-Roman antiquity to construct a civilizational clash between a "white Western" world and Asia, especially China. He contrasts this with a Milan exhibition, "Global Antiquity," which he says demonstrates that the ancient world was in fact a globalized, culturally intermixed era - the opposite of the picture these tech and political figures promote. As the only source on this topic, there is no cross-publication contrast to draw; the piece stands as Maak's personal interpretive argument framing the tech elite's invocation of antiquity as a postglobalist ideological distortion of history.

6913.comparison_text:
Coverage of Democrats' strategy toward Trump after the midterm wave comes almost entirely from American outlets, with Los Angeles Times offering the most extensive and varied treatment. One Los Angeles Times report describes House Democratic leaders prioritizing corruption investigations and affordability issues over impeachment, explicitly drawing lessons from the failures of the Pelosi-era impeachment battles. A separate Los Angeles Times piece by Jonathan J. Cooper and Lisa Mascaro takes a quite different angle, describing Democratic lawmakers' efforts to flatter Trump's vanity and dealmaking instincts to advance priorities like healthcare reform, while noting the mixed prospects given his unpredictability and his base's resistance to bipartisanship. A third Los Angeles Times article, by Mary Clare Jalonick, covers a related but distinct struggle - the Senate Democratic leadership fight between Van Hollen and Schumer - tying it partly to criticism of Schumer's stance on Israel and Gaza alongside broader generational tensions within the party.
In a column for Süddeutsche Zeitung, Peter Burghardt frames the same post-midterm choice in more analytical, historically grounded terms, arguing Democrats must decide between pursuing revenge against Trump officials and focusing on legislation, and warning that impeachment drives have historically failed and would do nothing to lower costs on their own - a view that aligns with the Los Angeles Times reporting favoring investigation over impeachment.
USA Today adds a complementary angle, detailing Democrats' legislative wish list - including ending the war with Iran, reversing Medicaid cuts, and banning congressional stock trading - while emphasizing internal tension between moderate and progressive factions.
The Washington Post, in a piece by Patrick Marley and Maegan Vazquez, covers a related but separate story: renewed momentum for abolishing the electoral college after the "blue wave," presenting arguments on both sides without tying it directly to the immediate political fight against Trump, in contrast to the more tactical focus of the other pieces.

6914.topic_label: FIFA presidency politics and Trump ties
6914.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column for Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Tammo Blomberg argues that FIFA president Gianni Infantino faces mounting scandal over alleged financial favors, including tax payments and luxury transport, yet is unlikely to be unseated. Blomberg attributes this to what he calls the president's "Trump advantage" - his close personal relationship with Donald Trump - combined with FIFA's diffuse power structure spread across 211 member federations. He notes, however, that Democrats gaining influence in the US legislature could bring greater scrutiny to Infantino's ties with Trump.

6915.topic_label: Art auction and memory of Argentina's Dirty War
6915.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column in The Guardian, Jonathan Jones criticizes the Sotheby's sale of the Blaquier-Arrieta art collection, arguing that the glamour surrounding the auction obscures the fact that it was funded by a sugar magnate allegedly implicated in the forced disappearance of hundreds of people under Argentina's military dictatorship. He contends that the auction's celebration of beauty and provenance will enshrine the collection's legend in history while the alleged crimes of Blaquier and Ledesma are reduced to a mere footnote.

6916.topic_label: Musk's plan to merge SpaceX and Tesla
6916.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a byline piece for Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Leonid Leiva Ariosa and Herbie Schmidt examine Elon Musk's reported plan to merge SpaceX and Tesla, arguing that the two companies' technologies could be complementary. At the same time, the authors flag a significant obstacle: Tesla's factories in China, they write, could pose too great a risk for the US government given concerns over dual-use technology sanctions. The framing thus combines technological enthusiasm with a geopolitical and regulatory caveat, and there is no other source coverage to compare it against.

6917.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by Neue Zürcher Zeitung, in a piece built around an interview with Thomas Zurbuchen. The framing is twofold: on one hand a domestic Swiss critique arguing that the country fails to exploit its considerable talent and potential in space research, pointing specifically to recent budget cuts; on the other, a broader geopolitical warning that the militarization of space by the United States, Russia and China could, absent international rules and communication channels, escalate from an incident in orbit into a military conflict on Earth. Since no other source addresses this topic, there is no cross-source contrast to draw - the piece stands alone, combining a national policy critique with a wider strategic security warning.

6918.topic_label: Corporate power struggle at Hugo Boss
6918.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source, Neue Zürcher Zeitung, in a piece signed by Dieter Bachmann. The article frames the episode as a power struggle in which Hugo Boss CEO Daniel Grieder is being pushed into early retirement after British retail tycoon Mike Ashley's Frasers Group acquired a majority stake and installed its own loyalists, against the backdrop of a collapsing share price and missed targets. With no other newspaper covering the story, there is no cross-source contrast to draw - the sole angle presented is that of a German-Swiss business press account scrutinizing how British corporate ownership is reshaping leadership at a storied German fashion house.

6919.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes exclusively from Neue Zürcher Zeitung, which offers two complementary angles. In their joint report, Beatrice Bösiger and Renato Schatz describe the unprecedented rejection of the 2027 budget by parliament's finance committee, focusing on how the parties blame one another rather than compromise, with their demands diverging so sharply that they can no longer be reconciled - noting cuts touching, among many domestic budget items, aid to Ukraine and the contribution to the Council of Europe. By contrast, in a column in Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Matthias Venetz warns of the danger this political blockade poses, framing it as a threat to the "Swiss success model" itself - moving beyond straight reporting on the political impasse toward a normative warning about its long-term consequences if no budgetary agreement can be reached.

6920.topic_label: Turkey: nationalism and sport under Erdoğan
6920.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a piece for Neue Zürcher Zeitung, Leon Scheffold and Seydi Kemer describe how Turkey's traditional oil-wrestling sport, Yağlı Güreş, has been politically appropriated by President Erdoğan and the AKP as a symbol of strength, discipline, and national tradition. The authors situate this within a broader pattern of authoritarian leaders using sporting spectacles for political image-building, noting that the proud, well-trained wrestlers embody an image of strength and discipline that aligns with the nationalist-conservative AKP's self-presentation.

6921.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic splits into quite distinct angles. The Daily Telegraph frames it as a direct competitive threat, arguing that China's cheap, open-source AI models endanger US dominance built on Nvidia chips and a handful of concentrated tech firms. In a column for Die Welt, Hannah Bethke takes a very different approach, drawing a parallel between the resurgence of nuclear deterrence logic amid Russia's war on Ukraine and the US-China AI race, warning that both arms races, driven by mutual fear and fear of falling behind China, undermine rather than ensure security. Writing in Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Niklas Maak offers a cultural-ideological angle, arguing that American tech billionaires and politicians such as Rubio, Vance, Thiel, Musk and Bezos are instrumentalizing a mythologized vision of classical antiquity to construct a civilizational clash between a "white West" and Asia or China, contrasting this with what he presents as antiquity's actual globalized, intermixed character. Separately, two articles address the infrastructure dimension of the rivalry - data center construction: also in Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Tim Schellenbach reports on a US midterm backlash against new data centers and asks whether similar resistance could spread to Germany, while Karen Weise in the Globe and Mail covers the same American backlash but concludes that most planned projects will proceed anyway due to existing permits and continued demand. Finally, in a separate Globe and Mail piece, Eric Reguly highlights Pope Leo XIV as what he calls the only prominent voice calling for restraint on the AI industry in the name of human dignity, against an industry skeptical that he can meaningfully slow Silicon Valley's unchecked growth.

6922.topic_label: Hito Steyerl's art and geopolitical critique
6922.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In an art review for Süddeutsche Zeitung, Till Briegleb discusses a retrospective of artist Hito Steyerl, arguing that her work exposes the hollowness of official promises of "security" and the violent, exploitative interests they conceal. Briegleb traces how Steyerl links German-Soviet gas deals from the 1970s, the 2022 sabotage of the Baltic pipeline, environmental destruction in Siberia, the disenfranchisement of local populations, Turkish military action against the Kurds, and German arms deliveries into a single continuum of false security narratives serving power and profit. Since no other source addresses this topic, there is no competing angle to compare - only Briegleb's detailed account of the broad geopolitical critique he sees embedded in Steyerl's art.

6923.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source here. In a column for Süddeutsche Zeitung, Boris Herrmann argues that a decade of obsessive global media fixation on Donald Trump has itself become part of the problem: keeping him at the center of attention, regardless of the subject, is precisely what fuels his power and sustains Trumpism. He calls for a deliberate collective "detox" from constant Trump coverage, framing the act of deliberately looking away as a strategic choice rather than mere media fatigue.

6924.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by The Globe and Mail, in a letters-to-the-editor section where several readers debate one another over whether Canada should adopt features of Sweden's or the Netherlands' health care systems. There is no single institutional stance here; rather it is an exchange among named letter writers, some of whom argue that privatization has produced worse outcomes, while others point to Sweden as achieving more with less spending, or note that the Netherlands and Denmark spend less than Canada yet achieve better results. Since these are signed letters rather than a staff-written article or editorial, the claims should be attributed to the individual letter writers rather than to The Globe and Mail as an institution.

6925.topic_label: Disability accessibility in Canadian medical workplaces
6925.comparison_text: This topic is covered only by The Globe and Mail, in a column by Michael Quon. He argues that disability among physicians is far more common than generally assumed, and that hospitals and medical institutions must make accessibility a systemic, permanent priority rather than leaving it to the advocacy of individual champions - a shift he frames as necessary to prevent skilled doctors from leaving the profession. With no other source addressing the issue, there is no competing framing or counter-view to compare it against.

6926.topic_label: Canadian pipeline expansion and environmental politics
6926.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column for The Globe and Mail, Mark Leiren-Young expresses frustration that even in British Columbia - long seen as a stronghold of environmental sentiment - public opinion has suddenly warmed to a pipeline expansion plan that could devastate the southern resident orca population. He argues that environmentalists are struggling to keep climate and conservation concerns politically salient while Prime Minister Carney pushes fossil fuel expansion yet still claims to uphold environmental values, and he calls for treating the economy, national sovereignty and environmental protection as interconnected rather than opposed, so that Canada's actual policies match the green image it projects abroad.

6927.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column for The Globe and Mail, Andrew Coyne pushes back against claims that the Carney government is "lying" about immigration figures, arguing that most people reclassified as "permanent" residents were already living in Canada on temporary status, meaning the actual net addition to the population from immigration is at historic lows. He further contends that public-opinion data show Canadians remain broadly supportive of immigration, despite loud rhetoric suggesting a "broken consensus" on the issue. With no other outlet weighing in, there is no competing framing to compare it against.

6928.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column in Süddeutsche Zeitung, Helmut Mauró portrays Daniel Barenboim's West-Eastern Divan project, which brings together Israeli and Palestinian musicians, as a resilient artistic and political undertaking that has endured decades of wars, political obstacles, and criticism. Mauró foregrounds Barenboim's enduring commitment to full freedom and equality between Israelis and Palestinians, quoting Barenboim's own words to frame the shared music-making as grounded in that aspiration, presenting the project as a symbol of possible coexistence amid ongoing conflict.

6929.topic_label: AI-generated images distorting climate change perception
6929.comparison_text: This topic is covered by a single source. In a column for Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Adrian Lobe argues that AI image generators distort public perception of the climate crisis by producing either apocalyptic fantasy imagery or saccharine "fun in the sun" clichés, both of which render invisible the real human stakes and dangers involved. He contends that such images are exploited by both climate activists and climate deniers alike, reinforcing pre-existing visual misrepresentations of climate risk rather than correcting them.

6930.comparison_text: Coverage of this topic comes from a single source, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, in a piece signed by Wolfgang Sandner. Rather than offering the newspaper's own institutional stance, the article relays the analysis of historian Gábor Erdődy, who argues that Viktor Orbán's sixteen years in power systematically dismantled university autonomy and cultural independence in Hungary, constructing what he calls an "illiberal democracy" through financial control and cronyism. Erdődy nonetheless voices cautious optimism that a new, Magyar party-led government could restore democratic rule of law. With no other source weighing in, there is no competing framing to compare - only this one historian's critical assessment as presented in a German newspaper.

6931.topic_label: Fall of Nvidia's Jensen Huang and the Chinese espionage scandal
6931.comparison_text: Coverage of Jensen Huang's downfall splits along distinct emphases. The Daily Telegraph's Poppy Wood centers on infighting within the Trump administration over blame for failing to blacklist Megaspeed despite intelligence warnings, quoting accusations that Commerce Secretary Lutnick "sold out our national security to keep the stock market high"; in a separate Daily Telegraph column, Andrew Orlowski frames the affair as entangled with a broader domestic ideological fight between AI "accelerationists" like Trump and Musk and "safetyists" like Anthropic and the Democrats. Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung runs an unusually extensive cluster: Roland Lindner argues the scandal reflects Huang's "alarming lack of judgment" and separately covers the succession race at Nvidia; Hendrik Ankenbrand examines the geopolitical risk to Singapore's standing as a trusted tech hub; Fabian Flotho and Maximilian Sachse broaden the lens to warn that Chinese "honey trap" espionage threatens German executives too; and a jointly bylined chronicle by Stephan Finsterbusch, Roland Lindner and Gustav Theile traces Huang's rise and fall, stressing his dual ties to both Trump and Beijing. Separately, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung's coverage citing Le Figaro warns of systemic financial risk from Nvidia's centrality, while another piece citing the Financial Times focuses on the dangers of Silicon Valley's unchecked "founder mode" culture. Die Welt's Benedikt Fuest, in his column, argues the episode exposes the structural "key-man risk" of AI giants run by overpowerful founders without succession plans. The Globe and Mail offers multiple angles: Joe Castaldo and Murad Hemmadi treat the ouster as a test case for "key man risk" in tech; in a column, John Rapley argues Huang's personal scandal shows how dangerously central he had become to both the AI boom and Trump's softer China policy; another report covers the Treasury secretary's public criticism of delayed export curbs; a reporting team examines how Asia loses its AI "ambassador" in Washington; and columnist David Berman links the affair to AI's wavering market narrative. Los Angeles Times contributes a distinctive historical framing through Jenny Jarvie and Richard Winton's piece on the enduring effectiveness of honey traps, alongside separate reports on congressional chip-export legislation and scrutiny of Lutnick over potential conflicts of interest. The Washington Post offers the deepest intelligence-political angle: one report describes how Marco Rubio and national security hawks used a CIA report on Huang's alleged ties to undermine his influence over Trump; another documents open clashes among Trump's economic advisers over Lutnick's handling of the affair; and a third traces years of effort by China hawks to curb Huang's sway before finally forcing him out. The Guardian focuses on public political pressure on Lutnick and congressional demands for transparency from Nvidia's board. Neue Zürcher Zeitung likewise offers two angles: Michael Rasch chronicles Huang's final days atop Nvidia while linking the personal scandal to the broader US-China tech rivalry, and a separate piece widens the lens to growing concern over Chinese espionage reaching into Switzerland itself.

6932.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Mahan argues California lacks legal tools to compel treatment for the most vulnerable unhoused residents and calls for expanding treatment beds and allowing involuntary treatment through CARE Court. Key excerpt: "We have to acknowledge that some of the people on our streets, often the ones who have languished the longest, are no longer able to make a rational decision regarding their own well-being."

6933.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Disputes the claim that war could have been avoided by granting Russia's demands, arguing Putin's NATO concerns were a smokescreen and that Russia violated Ukrainian sovereignty and international law. Key excerpt: "Mr. Putin's demands were a smokescreen. More than one million dead or wounded because Mr. Putin refuses to respect Ukrainian borders and international law."

6934.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Die Autorin argumentiert, dass ein vertiefter Wirklichkeits- und Möglichkeitssinn uns dazu bringen sollte, Flüsse nicht als auszubeutende Objekte, sondern als gleichwertige Subjekte mit eigenen Rechten zu begreifen, wie es indigene Gemeinschaften längst tun und wie es Bewegungen von Neuseeland bis Spanien inzwischen rechtlich umsetzen. Key excerpt: "2017 erhob Neuseeland den Whanganui als ersten Fluss weltweit zur Rechtsperson"

6935.topic_label: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's fall amid spy scandal and US-China tech rivalry
6935.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): The piece portrays Jensen Huang as a once-worshipped tech icon brought down by hubris, caught between US-China geopolitical rivalry over AI chips, implicated in alleged espionage via a Chinese mistress and chip-smuggling scheme, with Trump's administration itself under scrutiny for its handling of export controls and the affair. Key excerpt: "Es geht um einen Manager, der in eine sogenannte Honigfalle tappte. Um eine dubiose Firma, die kartonweise Nvidia-Chips nach China geschmuggelt haben soll. Und um die Systemrivalität der Supermächte China und USA, die längst auch mit jenen Chips ausgefochten wird, die Nvidia entwickelt."

6936.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Faktischer Bericht über die Verleihung des Magnitsky-Menschenrechtspreises an den inhaftierten, zum Tode verurteilten iranischen Boxer Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, der wegen seines Engagements für einen freien Iran verfolgt wird. Key excerpt: "Demnach akzeptierte vafaei Sani den Preis für „alle, die wegen des ‚verbechens‘ einen freien Iran anzustreben, einsitzen, gefoltert werden, bedroht werden und zum Tod verurteilt werden“."

6937.topic_label: Europäische Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, Kapitalmärkte und transatlantische Beziehungen
6937.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Kukies argumentiert, Europa sei im globalen Wettbewerb um Kapital und KI-Investitionen gegenüber den USA und China ins Hintertreffen geraten, sieht aber positive Signale durch deutsche Rentenreformen und bleibt optimistisch zu Frankreichs Wirtschaft trotz politischer Risiken wie einer möglichen Le-Pen-Präsidentschaft. Key excerpt: "Im Vergleich zu den beiden großen Machtblöcken China und USA hat Europa in Sachen Wettbewerbsfähigkeit leider noch immer nicht den Schritt vom Reden zum Machen geschafft."

6938.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Analyzes Defence Minister Pistorius's political maneuvering beyond his ministry, arguing he is positioning himself as a potential SPD chancellor candidate while downplaying Bundeswehr personnel shortages for political reasons, risking his credibility. Key excerpt: "Wer die Wirklichkeit in der Truppe politisch zurechtfärbt, verspielt jene Glaubwürdigkeit, die er in der Öffentlichkeit so erfolgreich aufgebaut hat."

6939.topic_label: UK Afghanistan SAS inquiry / national security
6939.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): A former SAS brigadier argues that the public inquiry into alleged unlawful killings in Afghanistan has been subject to media bias and risks exposing SAS personnel and their families to real danger from hostile state and non-state actors exploiting the proceedings. Key excerpt: "Without doubt, hostile state actors will have taken special interest in the inquiry as it provides them with a perfect hybrid opportunity to weaken a key Special Forces opponent."

6940.topic_label: Global power politics / history of hard and soft power
6940.comparison_text: Additional coverage (not merged into a cross-source comparison): Moore argues that sea power and hard military power historically underpin national dominance and the soft-power institutions (UN, IMF, NATO, etc) that followed WWII, warning that the West risks losing this hard power to illegitimate actors like Musk and Trump while Europe indulges in complacent overreach. Key excerpt: "hard and soft need each other but hard comes first"
